style_in_plain_words: A hazy, golden German-style wheat beer with a tall, dense white head. Typically it smells of banana and clove, and it is soft and creamy rather than bitter.
role_on_the_list: The proof beer: the one used to test whether the whole beer program is credible.
flavor_intent: Soft wheat bread, gentle banana and clove from the yeast, very little bitterness.
food_role: Lively bubbles cut through rich or fatty dishes, the clove note echoes warm spice, and low bitterness stays out of the way of heat. Goat birria and butter chicken quesadilla are the planned first matches (hypotheses, not tasted).
why_it_earns_a_tap: It is the beer most dependent on yeast character, so it is the clearest test of whether a brewing partner can deliver something distinctive. Its short, warm production cycle may also free tank time.
what_remains_undecided: The brewer decides the yeast strain, fermentation temperature and pitch, whether a rest step is worth it, open or closed fermentation, how much haze and sediment to keep, and the pass/fail thresholds for each proof. Any clarifying aid must be free of animal products (no isinglass; nothing from beef or pork).
status_plain: Design brief only. Not brewed, not tested, no recipe. A qualified brewer must develop it. The gate rule is PROPOSED decision D-77, which the founder has not yet confirmed.
non_brewer_note: Under proposed D-77 this is the proof beer, judged on six things (credibility, difference from the others, repeat drinkability, food fit, fermentation reliability, taproom appeal) with four outcomes: continue, revise, de-prioritise or remove. A brewer sets the thresholds, and a Hefeweizen failure would not by itself stop the other pilots. D-77 is not yet confirmed. Contains wheat and gluten; no gluten-free claim.

style_in_plain_words: A pale, very clear, light and fairly dry lager with a small white head. It is made to be crisp and easy to drink cold.
role_on_the_list: The everyday session beer for chile-forward food, and the planned largest share of volume.
flavor_intent: Light cracker-like malt, clean and dry, bitterness kept low so it does not push heat higher.
food_role: Cold, light and low in bitterness, so it gives relief from heat without adding to it. Chicken 65 totopos is the planned first match (a hypothesis, not tasted); it is expected to look thin beside very rich dishes like goat birria.
why_it_earns_a_tap: Chile-forward food needs a refreshing default, and a clean easy beer gives guests a simple starting point.
what_remains_undecided: The brewer decides whether any corn or grits earns its place, how long to lager, the water treatment, protection against light damage, and where in the style range the bitterness sits. Whether to list it AND the Pilsner or only one is a real open question: they may draw different guests or the same guests, they may suit different foods or the same foods, the Pilsner may need more tank time, each may take sales from the other, and the tap slot might have a better use. No answer is given here; the evidence (tastings, brewer input, sales) does not exist yet.
status_plain: Design brief only. Not brewed, not tested, no recipe. A qualified brewer must develop it.
non_brewer_note: If its bitterness is set toward the higher end, it starts to look like the Pilsner, which is why the two need a side-by-side tasting. Lime is not added by default. It is made from barley, so it is not gluten-free.

style_in_plain_words: A clear copper-amber lager with an off-white head, medium body and a toasted-bread malt flavour. It has no roasted or burnt taste.
role_on_the_list: The pairing workhorse for charred, smoky and slow-cooked dishes.
flavor_intent: Toasted bread crust and a little light caramel, clean, not sweet.
food_role: The toasty malt meets char and smoke and bridges to rich sauces. Goat birria and butter chicken quesadilla are the planned matches (hypotheses, not tasted); sweetness could become cloying with some dishes.
why_it_earns_a_tap: It gives the list a darker, malty choice that is not heavy, and it is the most different from the lighter lagers.
what_remains_undecided: The brewer decides the malt mix and balance so it stays dry rather than sweet, the lagering time, and the serving temperature (the traditional way is warmer than the cold default, so both should be tried).
status_plain: Design brief only. Not brewed, not tested, no recipe. A qualified brewer must develop it.
non_brewer_note: Expected to have a smaller default audience than the light lagers, so its tap case rests on food fit. It is made from barley, so it is not gluten-free.

style_in_plain_words: A clear golden lager with a dense white head, crisp and dry, with a noticeable but clean bitterness and a flowery or herbal hop aroma.
role_on_the_list: The beer that shows a brewer's skill. It is the snappy, dry lager that the Mexican-Style Lager is deliberately not.
flavor_intent: Bready pale malt, a firm clean bitterness and gentle floral or herbal hops.
food_role: Bitterness resets the palate between bites of fried and rich food. Gobi taco and chicken 65 totopos are the planned matches (hypotheses, not tasted); bitterness can also make heat feel stronger.
why_it_earns_a_tap: If a panel can tell it apart from the Mexican-Style Lager, it adds a second, sharper lager lane and a quality signal that flaws cannot hide behind.
what_remains_undecided: The brewer decides hop choice and cost, how the local water suits the style (the water numbers in the repo are unverified and need a lab test), clarity and filtering, lagering time, and a warmer serving arm. Whether to list it AND the Mexican-Style Lager or only one is a real open question: different guests or not, different foods or not, the longest tank time against a style that may sell more, mutual cannibalisation, and whether the slot has a better use. No verdict is given; the blind side-by-side tasting and sales evidence do not exist yet.
status_plain: Design brief only. Not brewed, not tested, no recipe. A qualified brewer must develop it.
non_brewer_note: Style-typical descriptions only. Hop supply and cost are unchecked. It is made from barley, so it is not gluten-free.

style_in_plain_words: A hazy, pale, soft Belgian-style wheat beer, traditionally brewed with coriander and orange peel for a light citrus aroma.
role_on_the_list: A seasonal beer for the warm months, a citrusy choice for paneer, vegetables and char.
flavor_intent: Soft wheat and oats, light orange and coriander aroma, gentle and refreshing.
food_role: Citrus lifts char and creamy yogurt and links to cilantro and lime. Paneer tikka taco is the planned match (a hypothesis, not tasted); with some dishes the citrus could turn soapy.
why_it_earns_a_tap: It gives guests a lighter, fragrant option that suits vegetable dishes and has a natural place in warm weather.
what_remains_undecided: The brewer decides the spice amount and timing, the peel source, how to keep the haze stable, how to avoid yeast cross-contamination with the Hefeweizen, and whether it is worth a slot. It overlaps the Hefeweizen as a wheat beer.
status_plain: Design brief only. Not brewed, not tested, no recipe. A qualified brewer must develop it.
non_brewer_note: Spices are style-typical aroma ingredients only, never added just to look Indian. Contains wheat and gluten, and coriander must be labelled. Its brief was written after the others, so it is the least developed.
